title: Social media engagement, perpetuating selected information, and accuracy regarding CA SB-201: Treatment or intervention on the sex characteristics of a minor
screen_reason: Content analysis of the 20 most-shared social media articles about California Senate Bill SB-201 (identified with BuzzSumo across Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest and Reddit in two one-month-before/after windows). Three urologist reviewers judged each article's factual accuracy against the peer-reviewed medical literature and the bill text, reporting 65% (13/20) misleading and 0% inaccurate. That is a share of items classified false/misleading against an external ground truth with a stated denominator, i.e. CONTENT prevalence.

estimates.country: United States (California Senate Bill SB-201; BuzzSumo searched worldwide social media engagement, but all 20 articles are US outlets: CNN, Apple News, Vice News, Breitbart, Huffington Post, The Blaze, Rewire News, Bay Area Reporter, Them., Oregon Live, Highlander News, San Francisco Chronicle, Snopes, LGBTQ Nation, Jefferson Public Radio, Gay Star News, Southern California Public Radio, San Francisco Examiner, YouTube, The Pride)
estimates.platform: Articles shared on Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest and Reddit, identified via BuzzSumo
estimates.date: Two windows: 31 December 2018 - 3 March 2019 (one month either side of the 31 January 2019 bill introduction) and 13 December 2019 - 13 February 2020 (one month either side of the 13 January 2020 final hearing)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-shared social media articles about SB-201 judged MISLEADING in terms of factual accuracy (containing both accurate and inaccurate information)
estimates.value_raw: Sixty-five percent (13/20) were misleading in terms of factual accuracy
estimates.denominator: 20 unique articles: the top 10 most-shared articles (by BuzzSumo engagement across Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest and Reddit) from each of two peak-activity windows around the introduction and the hearing of SB-201; 18 news and 2 editorial
estimates.definition: Article classified 'Misleading' = it 'included both accurate and inaccurate information'; 'Accurate' = 90% or more of the data presented was consistent with the peer-reviewed medical literature (and, for the bill description, with the text of the bill); 'Inaccurate' = 90% or more of statements not supported by published scientific literature
estimates.misinfo_def: 'Misinformation in the media can be harmful to patients and the general public'; operationalised as statements inconsistent with 'scientific information available in the peer-reviewed medical literature' and with 'the text of the bill'
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 375; Table 1 summary row ('65% Misleading 35% Accurate'); Abstract Results
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three researchers independently reviewed each article: two board-certified pediatric urologists and one urology resident, using a set review-question list (Appendix A) and 90%-consistency thresholds against the peer-reviewed medical literature and the bill text. The authors state they did NOT use a formal rubric or a validated questionnaire and made 'professional judgements of accuracy'; no inter-rater reliability statistic and no adjudication rule is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: We used four search terms "SB 201", "intersex", "DSD", and "surgery ban" and identified the top 10 most shared articles on social media platforms (Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest, and Reedit). We selected two time periods. ... The top ten articles with the highest engagement from each time point were then cataloged and reviewed.
estimates.notes: CONTENT, not QUALITY: the 'misleading' label REQUIRES inaccurate content ('included both accurate and inaccurate information'), so a wholly true article cannot receive it - this passes the INSTRUCTIONS' CONTENT test. CONTENT, not SHARING: the denominator is 20 articles, not shares; sharing engagement was only the selection rule, hence denom_selection=curated (top-10 most shared per window). topic=health_other because the accuracy judgement is medical (DSD incidence, medical necessity, surgical indications), although the subject is a legislative debate - an adjudicator could argue politics_elections. population_scope=other because the content producers are news and editorial organisations, not individual members of the public. year=2019 as the representative point of a collection period spanning Dec 2018 - Feb 2020.  QUOTE NOTE: the v2 text extraction interleaves the article's columns, so no longer contiguous span of the published sentence is recoverable; source_quote is the exact contiguous span carrying the value, and the full published sentence is: "None of the articles were considered inaccurate. Sixty-five percent (13/20) were misleading in terms of factual accuracy." (Results, p. 375); the Table 1 summary row reads "65% Misleading 35% Accurate".

estimates.platform: Articles shared on Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest and Reddit, identified via BuzzSumo
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-shared social media articles about SB-201 judged INACCURATE (90% or more of statements unsupported by the scientific literature) - the strict definition
estimates.value_raw: None of the articles were considered inaccurate (0/20)
estimates.definition: Article classified 'Inaccurate' = contained 90% or more statements not supported by published scientific literature (or, for the bill description, not consistent with the bill's text)
estimates.misinfo_def: Same 90%-threshold accuracy scheme as the misleading row
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 375; Table 1 (Accuracy of information represented column has only 'Misleading' and 'Accurate' values)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same three urologist reviewers and the same 90%-consistency thresholds; no reliability statistics reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Articles were classified as scientifically accurate if 90% or more of the data presented was consistent with scientific information available in the peer-reviewed medical literature. Misleading articles were those that included both accurate and inaccurate information. Inaccurate articles were those that contained 90% or more statements not supported by published scientific literature.
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR: this row exists to record the DEFINITION SENSITIVITY in a single paper - the same 20 articles yield 65% under the broad 'misleading' definition and 0% under the strict 'inaccurate' definition. The zero is stated verbatim ('None of the articles were considered inaccurate'), so it is a legitimate value, not a computed complement. definition_variant=true; do not pool with the 65% row.  QUOTE NOTE: the v2 text extraction interleaves the article's columns, so no longer contiguous span of the published sentence is recoverable; source_quote is the exact contiguous span carrying the value, and the full published sentence is: "None of the articles were considered inaccurate." (Results, p. 375) - the words "None of the articles were" sit on the preceding extracted line, mixed with the adjacent column, so the contiguous span used here starts at "considered inaccurate".

missed_or_uncertain: (1) '60% (12/20) were categorized as perpetuating selected information related to the authors' opinions' and '50% (n = 10) were classified as one-sided' are bias/balance measures, not veracity judgements: a wholly TRUE article can be one-sided or source-selective, so by the INSTRUCTIONS these are QUALITY-type constructs. They were not given rows because they measure framing rather than accuracy; an adjudicator wanting a QUALITY row could use 60% (12/20) perpetuating selected information. (2) 'Six articles (30%) cited the same statistic of intersex individuals making up 1-2% of the population' and 'Twenty-five percent of the articles in our study cited a similar figure regarding the incidence of DSD' are two apparently conflicting counts (30% vs 25%) for what looks like the same claim; the Discussion argues that citing that incidence figure is misleading, but neither is presented as the paper's misinformation prevalence, and the inconsistency makes both unusable. (3) 'The accurate articles had a median engagement of 657, compared to a median engagement of 2100 from the misleading articles' is a relative engagement comparison with no share of engagement attributable to misinformation, so no SHARING or CONCENTRATION row can be built (R1 fails: no group%/share% pair). (4) Coverage/omission counts (45% defined medical necessity, 45% described negative consequences, 85% discussed psychosocial concerns, 95% included a photograph, 75% quoted advocacy groups, 45% quoted a urologist) describe content composition, not falsity. (5) '67% of Americans in 2017 acquiring news from social media' (Pew, ref 20) and 'inaccurate articles were 28 times more likely to be shared' (Alsyouf et al., ref 21) are figures cited from elsewhere and are excluded by R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of 20 articles; no human subjects, no IRB required. Frame: BuzzSumo search on four terms ('SB 201', 'intersex', 'DSD', 'surgery ban') for links shared on Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest and Reddit, in two windows (one month either side of the 31 Jan 2019 introduction and of the 13 Jan 2020 hearing); the top 10 by engagement in each window were reviewed (20 unique articles, median engagement 1450, range 31-7200). Coding: three independent reviewers (two board-certified pediatric urologists, one urology resident) against the peer-reviewed medical literature and the bill text, with 90% thresholds for accurate/inaccurate and 'misleading' for mixed content; additional categories for balance, selected information, terminology, quoted sources. NO validated instrument, NO formal rubric, NO inter-rater reliability statistic and no stated disagreement-resolution procedure - the authors acknowledge personal bias could not be eliminated and say they mitigated it only by using multiple reviewers. Other stated limitations: BuzzSumo covers only some platforms; sharers' demographics and stance are unknown; sharing may reflect controversy rather than endorsement. Very small denominator (n=20), so each article moves the estimate by 5 percentage points.
